outputs.L1:
WASHINGTON (CNN) — As President Obama nears the 100th day of his administration, some in Washington are warning that the ongoing tug-of-war over torture could become a costly distraction.

Leg restraints await detainees at Guantanamo Bay in this 2006 photo.

Earlier this month, the Obama administration released four Bush-era memos detailing the “enhanced interrogation” of suspected al Qaeda members. The White House is now reviewing former Vice President Dick Cheney’s request to make additional memos public.

Two weeks before Obama released any memos, Cheney submitted a request to the National Archives seeking the release of other documents. He says the materials he requested will prove that the Bush administration’s interrogation tactics—which critics have described as a torture program—were effective.

“I haven’t talked about it, but I know specifically of reports that I read, that I saw, that lay out what we learned through the interrogation process and what the consequences were for the country,” Cheney said in an interview with Fox News last week.

The White House has signaled that it is not only considering Cheney’s request but may go even further.

“I think the president, as you know, is a big believer in transparency,” White House press secretary Robert Gibbs said Sunday on NBC’s “Meet the Press.” “I think one of the things that will have to be examined is whether there are additional memos that have to be released that give a broader picture of what’s gone on in enhanced interrogation techniques.”

The near-daily revelations are dividing Democrats between those calling for full disclosure and those urging caution.

“We don’t just turn the page without reading it. We want to make sure what the mistakes were so that the Obama administration doesn’t make these mistakes,” Sen. Patrick Leahy, D-Vermont, said Sunday.

But Sen. Dianne Feinstein, D-California, warned Sunday against moving too quickly.

“We need to find these things out, and we need to do it in a way that’s calm and deliberative and professional, because I think all of this, on the front burner, before the public, does harm our intelligence gathering, it does harm America’s position in the world,” she said on CNN’s “State of the Union.”

Across the aisle, Republicans are insisting that the Justice Department drop any investigation of Bush administration officials who authorized harsh interrogations.

“I think that would be a stab in the back. I think he has already demoralized the CIA, put them in a CYA mode,” Sen. Kit Bond, R-Missouri, said Sunday on Fox News.

Arizona Sen. John McCain, the former Republican presidential candidate, said prosecuting those who provided legal advice would be wrong.

“I don’t think those memos should have been released, but the fundamental point now is whether to prosecute people who gave the president, in my view, legitimate advice, even though it was wrong,” he said. “We should not be prosecuting people who gave legal advice. It’s wrong to do that to them, and it sets a terrible precedent for the future.”

Rep. Pete Hoekstra of Michigan, the top Republican on the House Intelligence Committee, and House Minority Leader John Boehner of Ohio are calling on the White House to release a list of those briefed on the interrogation programs.

“Congress and the American people deserve a full and complete set of facts about what information was yielded by CIA’s interrogation program, and they deserve to know which of their representatives in Congress were briefed about these techniques and the extent of those briefings,” Boehner said in a statement Monday.

“To date, the administration has fallen short in providing this information. ... The American people have been provided an incomplete picture of exactly what intelligence was made available by the interrogation program,” he said.

But Connecticut Sen. Joe Lieberman, a Democrat-turned-independent, said the entire debate over the memos is “moot.”

“What do we gain, first, by releasing the memos; but, secondly, what do we gain from indicting lawyers for their opinions, if that is a possibility here? ... It will poison the water here in Washington. It will achieve nothing. It will make it harder for President Obama to do some of the big things he wants to do for the country,” he said.

A 2006 photo shows leg restraints prepared for detainees at Guantanamo Bay.

Cheney filed that request with the National Archives two weeks before Obama released the initial set of documents. He argues that the records he wants disclosed will show that the Bush administration’s interrogation methods — labeled by critics as a torture program — were effective.

“I haven’t talked about it, but I know specifically of reports that I read, that I saw, that lay out what we learned through the interrogation process and what the consequences were for the country,” Cheney said last week during an interview with Fox News.

The White House has indicated that it may not only consider Cheney’s request but could potentially release even more material.

“I think the president, as you know, is a big believer in transparency,” White House press secretary Robert Gibbs said Sunday on NBC’s “Meet the Press.” “I think one of the things that will have to be examined is whether there are additional memos that have to be released that give a broader picture of what’s gone on in enhanced interrogation techniques.”

The near-daily disclosures are creating a split among Democrats, with some demanding full openness and others advising restraint.

“We don’t just turn the page without reading it. We want to make sure what the mistakes were so that the Obama administration doesn’t make these mistakes,” Sen. Patrick Leahy, a Vermont Democrat, said Sunday.

Sen. Dianne Feinstein, a California Democrat, cautioned Sunday that the process should not move too fast.

“We need to find these things out, and we need to do it in a way that’s calm and deliberative and professional, because I think all of this, on the front burner, before the public, does harm our intelligence gathering, it does harm America’s position in the world,” she said on CNN’s “State of the Union.”

Republicans, meanwhile, are pressing the Justice Department to abandon any inquiry into Bush administration officials who approved severe interrogation practices.

“I think that would be a stab in the back. I think he has already demoralized the CIA, put them in a CYA mode,” Sen. Kit Bond, a Missouri Republican, said Sunday on Fox News.

Sen. John McCain of Arizona, the former Republican presidential nominee, said it would be improper to prosecute people for providing legal guidance.

“I don’t think those memos should have been released, but the fundamental point now is whether to prosecute people who gave the president, in my view, legitimate advice, even though it was wrong,” McCain said. “We should not be prosecuting people who gave legal advice. It’s wrong to do that to them, and it sets a terrible precedent for the future.”

Rep. Pete Hoekstra of Michigan, the ranking Republican on the House Intelligence Committee, and House Minority Leader John Boehner of Ohio are urging the White House to disclose who in Congress received briefings on the interrogation programs.

“Congress and the American people deserve a full and complete set of facts about what information was yielded by CIA’s interrogation program, and they deserve to know which of their representatives in Congress were briefed about these techniques and the extent of those briefings,” Boehner said in a statement Monday.

“To date, the administration has fallen short in providing this information. ... The American people have been provided an incomplete picture of exactly what intelligence was made available by the interrogation program,” he added.

Connecticut Sen. Joe Lieberman, who left the Democratic Party to become an independent, said the dispute over the memos no longer serves a purpose.

“What do we gain, first, by releasing the memos; but, secondly, what do we gain from indicting lawyers for their opinions, if that is a possibility here? ... It will poison the water here in Washington. It will achieve nothing. It will make it harder for President Obama to do some of the big things he wants to do for the country,” Lieberman said.

Instead, it prompted new demands for additional documents, renewed criticism from Republicans, and growing disagreement among Democrats over how far the country should go in investigating the past.

One of the central questions was whether the administration should release more classified material, including memos requested by former Vice President Dick Cheney. His request put pressure on the Obama administration to decide whether transparency should extend not only to legal justifications for the interrogations, but also to intelligence assessments that supporters of the program claimed would defend it.

The controversy quickly became a political challenge for Obama. He had entered office promising to end practices he viewed as inconsistent with American values, including torture, and had moved to close the detention facility at Guantánamo Bay. At the same time, he was trying to keep public attention focused on urgent domestic priorities, especially the economic crisis, health care reform, and the broader effort to stabilize the financial system. A prolonged fight over interrogation policies threatened to consume Washington’s attention and complicate his early agenda.

Democrats were divided over the best course. Some lawmakers and activists argued that the country needed a full accounting of what had happened, including possible investigations into the officials who designed or approved the interrogation program. They said that transparency was necessary to restore the rule of law and ensure that similar abuses would not happen again. Others warned that moving too quickly toward investigations or prosecutions could appear partisan, deepen political divisions, and distract from more immediate national problems.

The White House sought to balance these competing pressures. Obama signaled that he wanted to look forward rather than backward, particularly when it came to CIA personnel who had relied on legal guidance from the previous administration. But he also left open the possibility that higher-level officials who shaped the policies could face scrutiny. That position satisfied neither side completely: critics of the interrogation program wanted a stronger commitment to accountability, while defenders of the Bush administration accused Obama of endangering national security and politicizing intelligence.

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — The Obama administration is considering whether to release additional Bush-era documents detailing the results of harsh interrogation techniques used on terrorism suspects, after former Vice President Dick Cheney asked that more material be declassified to show the program produced valuable intelligence, White House officials said.

White House press secretary Robert Gibbs said the administration would review Cheney’s request through the normal declassification process, but he pushed back on the former vice president’s broader defense of the interrogation program.

“The president has made clear that these techniques are not consistent with our values,” Gibbs said, adding that any decision on releasing more records would be made carefully and with national security concerns in mind.

Cheney has argued that the Obama administration presented an incomplete picture when it released Justice Department memos authorizing enhanced interrogation methods, including waterboarding. He has said additional classified records would show that information obtained from detainees helped prevent attacks and save lives.

The debate has intensified on Capitol Hill, where lawmakers remain sharply divided over how far to go in investigating the CIA’s interrogation practices and whether releasing more documents would clarify the record or further politicize it.

Sen. Patrick Leahy, the Democratic chairman of the Senate Judiciary Committee, said the country needs a fuller accounting of what happened during the previous administration. Leahy has previously called for a “truth commission” to examine detainee treatment and the legal rationale behind the interrogation program.

Sen. Dianne Feinstein, the Democratic chairwoman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, said her panel would continue its review of the CIA program. Feinstein has said lawmakers must understand both what techniques were used and what intelligence, if any, they produced, while also protecting sensitive sources and methods.

Republicans, meanwhile, accused the Obama administration of selectively releasing documents that damaged the Bush administration while withholding records that might support its case.

Sen. Kit Bond, the top Republican on the Senate Intelligence Committee, said if the administration releases legal memos describing the techniques, it should also release documents showing the intelligence gained from them. Bond argued that Americans deserve to see the “full story,” not just portions that cast the program in the worst light.

Sen. John McCain, a Republican and former prisoner of war who has long opposed torture, warned against returning to interrogation methods he said violate American principles. McCain said the United States should not use techniques that it would condemn if used against U.S. service members, though he also urged a measured approach to any further disclosures.

House Republican Leader John Boehner said the release of the original memos had already raised concerns about national security and morale inside the intelligence community. Boehner said additional disclosures could make it harder for intelligence officers to do their jobs if they fear their actions may later become public and politicized.

Sen. Joe Lieberman, an independent who caucused with Democrats, said the government must strike a balance between transparency and protecting national security. Lieberman said the country should learn from past decisions but avoid steps that could compromise intelligence operations or deepen partisan divisions.

The administration’s deliberations come after President Barack Obama ordered an end to the CIA’s use of enhanced interrogation techniques and directed that interrogations follow the Army Field Manual. Obama has said the United States can keep the country safe without resorting to methods he considers torture.

At the same time, the White House has tried to contain the political fallout from the release of the Bush-era legal memos. Obama initially said CIA officers who relied on the Justice Department guidance should not be prosecuted, but he left open the possibility of review for those who crafted the legal opinions.

The question now before the administration is whether releasing more records would answer Cheney’s challenge — or prolong a contentious debate over national security, accountability and the limits of presidential power in the years after the September 11 attacks.

**Washington —** As President Barack Obama marked his first 100 days in office, a fierce debate over the Bush administration’s interrogation policies threatened to overshadow the new president’s broader agenda, reopening one of the most divisive national security disputes of the post-9/11 era.

The controversy intensified after the Obama administration released previously classified Justice Department memos that authorized harsh interrogation techniques used on suspected terrorists, including waterboarding, sleep deprivation and stress positions. The documents, written during the Bush administration, offered legal justification for methods critics have long described as torture.

Obama, who banned the use of such techniques shortly after taking office, said the United States must move forward while acknowledging what happened. He argued that the country’s security does not require abandoning its values, but he also expressed reluctance to pursue prosecutions of CIA officers who relied on government legal guidance.

“We have been through a dark and painful chapter in our history,” Obama said in remarks on the issue, emphasizing that his administration would reject torture while focusing on current security challenges.

Former Vice President Dick Cheney quickly became the most prominent defender of the Bush-era program. Cheney argued that enhanced interrogation techniques produced valuable intelligence and helped prevent additional attacks. He called for the release of more classified documents that he said would prove the effectiveness of the program.

Critics rejected that claim, saying the memos revealed a system designed to evade legal and moral limits. Human rights advocates and some Democratic lawmakers argued that the United States had an obligation to investigate how the interrogation program was approved and whether laws were broken.

On Capitol Hill, responses split sharply along political and ideological lines. Some Democrats called for hearings or an independent commission to examine the origins of the policies. Senator Patrick Leahy promoted the idea of a “truth commission,” while others said accountability was necessary to prevent similar practices in the future.

But not all Democrats embraced a broader inquiry. Some worried that a prolonged investigation could consume Washington, distract from the economic crisis and complicate Obama’s efforts to advance health care, financial reform and other priorities.

Republicans largely accused the administration of endangering national security by releasing the memos and second-guessing decisions made in the aftermath of the September 11 attacks. They argued that intelligence officers and policymakers were operating under extreme pressure to prevent another catastrophe.

The debate placed Obama in a politically delicate position. He had campaigned on restoring the rule of law and ending practices widely condemned abroad, but he also sought to avoid a backward-looking partisan battle. His administration initially said CIA personnel who followed legal advice would not face prosecution, while leaving open questions about whether the lawyers who drafted the memos or senior officials who approved the program could be scrutinized.

The dispute underscored the broader tension of Obama’s early presidency: a promise to break from the Bush era while managing wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, confronting terrorist threats and navigating a severe economic downturn.

As the first 100 days came to a close, the torture memos debate showed no sign of fading. Cheney’s public defense ensured that the argument over whether enhanced interrogation worked — and whether it should ever have been authorized — would remain a central fight in Washington’s reckoning with the legacy of 9/11.

---

**Release of Bush-Era Interrogation Documents Rekindles Debate Over Accountability**

*Washington* — The release of previously classified Bush administration documents detailing the legal rationale behind so-called “enhanced interrogation” techniques has reignited a fierce debate in Washington over whether former officials — including senior policymakers and government lawyers — should face formal investigation.

The documents, prepared in the years after the September 11 attacks, outline the administration’s justification for interrogation methods used by the CIA against terrorism suspects held in secret detention facilities overseas. Critics have long argued that the techniques amounted to torture and violated both U.S. and international law. Defenders say the program was authorized at the highest levels of government and was believed at the time to be lawful and necessary to prevent future attacks.

The newly released materials have intensified calls from human rights advocates and some lawmakers for a full inquiry into how the interrogation program was approved, who authorized it and whether the legal opinions supporting it were crafted to provide cover for policies already in motion.

“This is not simply about looking backward,” one civil liberties advocate said. “It is about whether the United States government can authorize abuse, conceal it behind legal memos and then declare the matter closed.”

Former Bush administration officials have pushed back sharply, arguing that the country was facing an unprecedented security threat and that decisions were made in good faith based on intelligence assessments and legal guidance. They warn that prosecuting or investigating officials over national security decisions could criminalize policy disagreements and chill future government decision-making.

At the center of the controversy are Justice Department lawyers who wrote memos concluding that certain harsh interrogation methods did not constitute torture under U.S. law. Those opinions were later withdrawn or superseded, but they played a key role in allowing the CIA program to move forward.

Legal experts remain divided over whether the authors of those memos should face professional discipline, congressional scrutiny or possible criminal investigation. Some argue that lawyers who knowingly distorted the law to authorize abusive conduct should not be shielded simply because they worked inside the government. Others say criminal liability would be difficult to prove, particularly if officials relied on formal legal opinions from the Justice Department’s Office of Legal Counsel.

The political stakes are significant. Supporters of an investigation say accountability is necessary to restore the rule of law and repair America’s standing abroad. Opponents contend that reopening the issue would be divisive, partisan and damaging to intelligence agencies still engaged in counterterrorism operations.

The debate also places current Justice Department leaders in a delicate position: whether to pursue a potentially explosive investigation into their predecessors or to maintain a forward-looking approach focused on preventing similar practices in the future.

Members of Congress have floated several options, including a special commission, expanded oversight hearings or referral of certain matters to the Justice Department’s internal watchdog. Some Democrats have said the public deserves a full accounting of the decisions that led to the program. Republicans, meanwhile, have accused critics of attempting to punish officials who acted to protect the country after 9/11.

The release of the documents does not by itself determine whether laws were broken. But it has ensured that one of the most contentious chapters of the post-9/11 era will remain part of the national conversation — raising enduring questions about executive power, wartime decision-making and the limits of legal justification in the face of national security threats.

He has urged the release of CIA assessments and other records that, in his view, would demonstrate that the program helped prevent terrorist attacks.

White House officials said the request is being examined through the normal declassification process, involving the CIA, Justice Department, National Security Council and other agencies. They cautioned that no final decision has been made and that some materials may remain classified to protect intelligence sources, methods and foreign partnerships.

“The president has been clear that he believes in transparency where possible and national security where necessary,” said a senior administration official, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss internal deliberations. “This request is being reviewed carefully, not politically.”

The review comes as the administration tries to balance competing pressures from lawmakers and advocacy groups. Many Democrats have called for a fuller accounting of the interrogation program, including possible investigations into whether laws were broken. Republicans have accused the White House of selectively releasing documents that cast Bush-era officials in the worst possible light while withholding evidence they say would support the program’s effectiveness. Independents and civil-liberties advocates have pressed for maximum disclosure but warned against using classified information as a partisan weapon.

Rep. Ellen Marshall, D-Calif., a member of the House Judiciary Committee, said the administration should release as much material as possible — but not simply to settle a political dispute with Cheney.

“If there are documents that explain what happened, the public deserves to see them,” Marshall said. “But transparency cannot mean cherry-picking records to justify conduct that may have violated American law and values. We need the full record, and we need to follow the facts wherever they lead.”

Sen. Richard Callahan, R-Texas, said the White House had created the controversy by releasing the legal memos while withholding other classified assessments.

“You cannot put half the story on the front page and then claim national security prevents the rest from being told,” Callahan said. “If the administration is going to release documents describing the interrogation methods, it should also release documents describing what intelligence was gained. The American people can handle the truth.”

Independent Sen. Thomas Reed of Maine said both parties risk turning intelligence decisions into political theater.

“The question should not be whether a document helps Democrats or Republicans,” Reed said. “The question is whether release serves the public interest without endangering ongoing operations, intelligence sources or our allies. That standard has to apply across the board.”

At issue are CIA records that Cheney has said would show interrogations of high-value detainees produced information about al-Qaida plots and operatives. Critics of the program dispute that claim, saying many experienced interrogators concluded that coercive methods were unreliable, unnecessary and damaging to U.S. credibility.

The debate intensified after President Barack Obama authorized the release of several Bush-era Office of Legal Counsel memos that provided the legal framework for the CIA program. Obama also said CIA officers who relied in good faith on Justice Department guidance would not be prosecuted, but he left open the possibility of scrutiny for policymakers who designed or approved the program.

That distinction has angered Republicans and disappointed some Democrats.

“The people who carried out legal guidance from the Department of Justice should not be scapegoated,” said Rep. Mark Hensley, R-Ariz. “But neither should senior officials be smeared after the fact for making difficult decisions in the aftermath of 9/11.”

Sen. Maria Alvarez, D-N.Y., said the administration cannot rule out prosecutions before reviewing the full record.

“No one is above the law,” Alvarez said. “If evidence shows that officials authorized torture or knowingly exceeded legal limits, then the Justice Department has an obligation to act independently. Transparency is not a substitute for accountability.”

Civil-liberties groups said releasing additional CIA documents could be valuable, but only if the administration avoids selective disclosure.

“A partial release designed to defend or condemn the program would only deepen public mistrust,” said Karen Holt, director of the nonpartisan Center for Constitutional Security. “The country needs a comprehensive accounting — what was authorized, what was done, what intelligence was obtained, and what the costs were to America’s standing in the world.”

Former intelligence officials are also divided. Some argue that the CIA’s interrogation program yielded important leads during a period when the government feared another catastrophic attack. Others say the harsh techniques damaged intelligence gathering by producing false information and undermining cooperation with foreign partners.

“The danger is that people will read an intelligence report and assume that because a detainee said something after harsh treatment, the technique worked,” said Paul Harrigan, a former intelligence analyst who now advises private clients. “In intelligence work, causation is hard to prove. Information often comes from multiple sources, and the paper trail can be misleading.”

National security veterans warned that releasing more documents could reveal sensitive details even if names and operational information are redacted.

“Declassification is not as simple as blacking out a few lines,” said Janet Wilkes, a former senior counterterrorism official. “Records can expose liaison relationships, interrogation timelines, detention locations and analytic judgments. Adversaries study these releases closely.”

White House press officials declined to say when the review would be completed. A CIA spokesman said the agency “continues to support appropriate declassification review consistent with the protection of national security.”

The Justice Department also faces pressure over whether to appoint a special prosecutor or otherwise investigate the origins of the interrogation program. Obama has repeatedly signaled reluctance to allow the issue to consume his young administration, saying the country should “look forward” even as it learns from the past. But that posture has satisfied few on either side.

For Cheney and his allies, the release of additional documents is a test of whether Obama’s transparency pledge applies to information that might complicate criticism of the Bush administration. For many Democrats, the request is an effort to relitigate and justify practices they regard as torture. For independents, the fight underscores the challenge of exposing government wrongdoing without compromising security or turning classified intelligence into partisan ammunition.

“The American people deserve more than slogans,” Reed said. “They deserve facts, accountability and a government that can protect them without abandoning the principles it claims to defend.”

For now, the decision rests with an administration trying to navigate a dispute inherited from its predecessor but now firmly on its own desk: how much of the secret history of the war on terror should be made public, and at what cost.

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a news article summarizing the 2009 debate over Guantanamo-era interrogation tactics, the release of Bush-era memos, and political warnings that the issue could distract from Obama’s agenda.
counterfactuals.output:
**Debate Over Bush-Era Interrogations Threatens to Complicate Obama Agenda**

*Washington, 2009* — The Obama administration’s decision to release once-secret Bush-era legal memos authorizing harsh interrogation tactics has reignited a fierce national debate over the treatment of terrorism suspects and raised concerns among Democrats that the controversy could distract from President Barack Obama’s broader domestic agenda.

The Justice Department documents, written by the Office of Legal Counsel during the George W. Bush administration, detailed the legal rationale used to approve interrogation methods employed by the CIA against detainees held after the September 11 attacks. The techniques included waterboarding, sleep deprivation, stress positions, confinement in small spaces and other methods critics have long described as torture.

Obama, who entered office pledging to close the Guantanamo Bay detention facility and end practices he said damaged America’s moral standing, said the release of the memos was intended to promote transparency and help the country move forward. At the same time, he signaled reluctance to pursue prosecutions of CIA personnel who relied on legal guidance from the previous administration.

“This is a time for reflection, not retribution,” Obama said in remarks at the time, arguing that the United States should not lose focus on economic recovery, health care reform and national security challenges.

But the publication of the memos quickly intensified partisan conflict. Human rights groups and some Democratic lawmakers called for investigations into how the interrogation program was approved and whether senior officials violated U.S. or international law. They argued that accountability was necessary to prevent similar abuses in the future.

Republicans and former Bush administration officials defended the interrogation program, saying it produced valuable intelligence and helped protect the country from additional terrorist attacks. Former Vice President Dick Cheney became one of the most prominent defenders of the policies, urging the release of documents he said would show the methods were effective.

The controversy also placed congressional Democrats under scrutiny. Questions emerged about what lawmakers had been told in classified briefings about the CIA program, prompting disputes over whether members of Congress had objected at the time or were now seeking political distance from decisions made in the aftermath of 9/11.

Inside Washington, some Obama allies warned that a prolonged fight over Bush-era national security policy could consume political energy needed for the president’s ambitious agenda. The administration was already grappling with the financial crisis, a major stimulus program, plans to overhaul health care and the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan.

Political strategists cautioned that hearings, investigations or a special commission could dominate headlines and deepen partisan divisions. They feared the issue might pull attention away from legislative priorities and complicate Obama’s effort to present himself as focused on the future rather than relitigating the past.

Still, the debate proved difficult to contain. For critics of the interrogation program, the memos were evidence of a deliberate legal effort to justify abusive treatment. For defenders, they were part of a difficult wartime record that should be judged in the context of fears following the September 11 attacks.

The dispute underscored one of the central tensions of Obama’s first year in office: how to break with the most controversial elements of the Bush administration’s counterterrorism policies while avoiding a politically consuming battle over accountability. As the White House sought to steer attention back to the economy and domestic reform, the legacy of Guantanamo, secret prisons and “enhanced interrogation” remained a powerful and divisive issue in American politics.
